The three-minute version

Cosmo

What it is, why it works the way it does, and what you need to try it. Seven questions, short answers.

So what is Cosmo?

It's a set of written guides (we call them skills), helper agents and a shared library of ready-made charts and slides, for AI assistants like Claude Code or Cursor.

You ask for a report, a deck or a dashboard in plain words. It comes out looking like everyone else's, and what the team learns along the way gets kept for next time.

Why build from a library instead of having the AI draw everything from scratch?

Because most of a report page is the same every time, and there's no point paying the assistant to rewrite it.

In one sample five-chart report, about 63% of the page was styling and chart code that never changes. The assistant itself wrote under about 1,000 tokens (a token is a chunk of text you pay for and wait on). That's one sample, not an average.

  • Every report has the same look.
  • New data means a rebuild, not a rewrite.
  • Less text written means less to pay for and less to wait for.

Want the details? How deliverables are built

Why do we use a script to make presentations?

Because a script does the fiddly parts the same way every time.

It copies a slide from the library, fills its chart from your data, and checks that nothing spills off the slide. Then you edit a few lines of wording.

  • Every deck looks the same.
  • When the numbers change, you refresh the deck instead of rebuilding it.
  • A mistake shows up in a check, not in the meeting.
How it works, step by step
  1. The assistant picks a slide from the library by its id.
  2. The script copies it into your deck and points its chart at your columns.
  3. It checks every slide for text or charts that overflow, and takes screenshots.
  4. You, or the assistant, edit the wording on the slide.

Want the details? How deliverables are built

What if the chart we want isn't quite in the library?

The closest one still goes in, with a note saying exactly what to change by hand. And when you end up with a chart you like, it gets saved back, so next time it's just there.

Two helpers handle this. One suggests which library items fit your request and says plainly what the library doesn't have. The other saves new visuals back into the library.

  • You never start from a blank page.
  • The library grows out of real work.

Want the details? How deliverables are built

Why does the assistant need a brain?

Because it starts every conversation knowing nothing about your team, your data or what you decided last week.

The brain is a folder of short notes it reads first, and it only reads the few that matter for what you asked. New facts get filed after the work, but only when you say yes.

  • You stop explaining the same background every time.
  • It reads a handful of notes, not the whole folder.
  • What one person learns, the whole team can use.

Want the details? How the brain works

Why hand work to helpers instead of one long chat?

Because a long chat re-reads everything at every step, so each step costs more than the one before.

Instead, one planner keeps the thread, and short helper chats on cheaper models do the building. In one worked example that came to roughly $1.00 against $2.20 for the same job in a single chat. That's an estimate, not a measured bill.

  • Cheaper in the example we worked through.
  • Each helper sees only what it needs, so it stays on task.
  • The planner checks every result before it's used.

Want the details? How the work is handed out

What do I need to start?

Not much. A setup page is on the way; for now, this is the list.

  • Claude Code or Cursor, signed in.
  • The Cosmo folder, copied into your assistant's settings folder.
  • Python and Node.js. The skills that build reports, decks and dashboards use them.
  • Edge or Chrome, so the assistant can look at what it made.
  • A folder of notes for the brain. Optional at first.

Idea 1 of 3

Deliverables

Reports, decks and dashboards, built from parts that already work.

What counts as a deliverable?

Three things, each with its own skill (a short written guide the assistant follows). You ask in plain words and the assistant picks the right one.

A report

The analysis skill explores a question, then writes it up as a web page when you say so. It doesn't build a view you open every week.

A slide deck

The presentation skill turns work that already exists into slides. It doesn't do the analysis, and it doesn't make PowerPoint files.

A dashboard

The dashboard skill makes a standing view with filters on live data. It isn't for a one-off story.

Why do we use a script to make them?

Say you want a chart of cost by region. The script copies a ready-made chart from our shared design library (a folder of charts, tables and slides) into one small file. It fills that file from your data and prints the few lines to reword. Then it checks that nothing is cut off.

  • The same look every time.
  • When the numbers change, you refresh. You don't redo the deck.
  • Problems show up in a check, not in the meeting.
How it works, step by step

  1. Read the library's list

    A short index, not every file.

  2. Pick items

    One chart, table or slide per point.

  3. Copy each in

    Each becomes one small file in your piece.

  4. Point it at your data

    Name the columns that feed it.

  5. Edit the few lines you want changed

    A title, a colour, a third line.

  6. Build and look

    It builds, takes a picture and checks it.

  7. Save one you like back

    It goes into the library for everyone.

Isn't it faster to ask the AI to write the whole page?

Not really, because most of a page is the same every time: the styling and the chart-drawing code. In one sample five-chart report, the page was about 23 KB, and about 63% of it was that unchanging code. The assistant's own writing was under about 1,000 tokens (a token is a chunk of text you pay and wait for).

23KBone finished five-chart page
63%of it code that never changes
25KBa library chart file
4KBthe part that gets copied

All of this is from one sample, so read it as an example, not a promise.

How do I know what a chart needs before I add it?

You ask to see it first. A show step prints just that item's parts: which ones are required, which of your columns fit each, and a ready-made command to copy it in. Every item has its own parts, so the list is different for each one.

What if the chart is close but not quite right?

It still goes in. If a part can't be filled from your data, it goes in on placeholder data with a MANUAL line saying exactly which line to edit by hand. A tweak to the look is usually a few lines in one file. The library covers common visuals, not every one.

Two helpers (subagents, each started for one job) take care of the rest. One suggests which items fit what you're making, and says plainly what the library doesn't have. The other saves a chart you like back into the library.

What happens when the data changes?

You rebuild. The figures in a report's text are pulled from the data, so they update on their own. Charts refill and keep your edits. A theme (one set of colours and fonts) changes the whole look with one command.

  • New data means a rebuild, not a rewrite.
  • Your hand edits stay.
  • A library item looks the same in a report, a deck and a dashboard.

Idea 2 of 3

The brain

A shared notebook the assistant reads before it answers.

Why does the assistant need a brain?

Because it starts every conversation knowing nothing about your work. So you explain the same things again: what a column means, which table to trust, why a number is defined that way. And when one person figures something out, it stays with them.

  • Explain a thing once, not every time.
  • What one person learns, the team gets.

So what is it, actually?

A folder of short note pages, one per topic, kept as plain files (markdown, if you know it). Some pages are yours alone. Others are shared with the team. Before the assistant answers, it reads the ones that matter.

The graph below is a made-up brain: each circle is a page, each line joins two related pages. Press the button to see what the assistant would open for a real question.

Example request

How has claims trend changed month over month?

Tap a circle to read what the page says.

What the assistant reads

  1. Nothing yet. Run the request to fill this in.

Nothing read yet.

Running the request lights up the pages that bear on trend, plus the lines between them, and dims the rest. The big circles are the pages most others link to.

Does it read the whole thing every time?

No. For a question about claims trend, the assistant above opens 11 of the 22 pages and leaves the rest closed. It picks pages by what they say about the question, and it opens only the part that applies.

  • Shorter conversations.
  • The same answer for everyone, because it comes from the same pages.

How does something get into the brain?

While you work, the assistant jots down facts worth keeping, one line each. Later, when you ask it to, it files each one onto the right personal page, or starts a new page if the topic has none. Sharing is your call: you pick which lines move to the team page.

How it works, step by step

  1. Something comes up

    The assistant notes it as one plain line.

  2. Intake files it

    It goes onto the right personal page.

  3. You share it

    Pick lines to move to the team page.

  4. Later sessions read it

    You or a colleague, on a similar task.

Four skills

A skill is a written guide the assistant follows.

  • brain-file files the facts noted so far. Only when you ask.
  • brain-ingest pulls facts out of documents you drop in a folder.
  • brain-promote moves lines you pick to the team page.
  • brain-cite lists the pages worth reading for your task.

Four helpers

A helper is a small assistant started for one job.

  • brain-filer decides where each fact goes and writes it.
  • brain-extractor finds the lasting facts in documents.
  • brain-promoter adds picked lines to the team page.
  • brain-context-analyst picks the few pages worth reading.

What goes in, and what stays out?

Things that stay true go in. Results, secrets and private details stay out.

In

  • Definitions and methods
  • How data and systems behave, and known traps
  • Decisions, and the reason for them

Out

  • A project's results They go in that project's findings.
  • Passwords, keys and other secrets
  • Personal details about people

The brain is only as good as what gets put in. Keep each fact short, say where it came from, and keep anything private out.

Idea 3 of 3

Orchestration

How one planner and a few helpers get a big job done.

Why not just do everything in one long chat?

For a small job, do. For a big one, the chat fills up its context window, which is how much it can hold in mind at once. Every new step makes it re-read the whole conversation, so it gets slower and costs more. And what you decided at the start gets buried.

So what's the idea?

You talk to one planner, the orchestrator. It splits the job up and hands each piece to a helper, a subagent, that starts with a fresh memory. The helper does the work and sends back a short report. The planner only ever reads the reports.

  • The chat you're in stays short and focused.
  • Pieces that don't overlap run at the same time.
  • Each helper can use the model that suits its job.

What does that look like on a real question?

Say you ask: "How has claims trend changed month over month, and is there a notable difference in the number of high-cost claimants?" Here's the run.

  1. The planner settles the definitions. Which date counts, paid or service? What counts as "high-cost"? Then it agrees a short plan with you.
  2. A small model looks at the data once. It reports the columns, the date range and the row count.
  3. Two builders work at the same time. One does the month-over-month trend, the other counts high-cost claimants. Each adds a chart from the design library.
  4. A checker re-runs both. It confirms the numbers in the text match the data.
  5. The planner writes the answer from the four short reports.

Why give helpers different models?

A model is the AI engine behind an assistant. Bigger ones think better but are slower and dearer, so using one for every little job is wasteful. We match the model to the work.

Small, fast

A quick look

Reading the data once and reporting what's in it.

Mid-sized

Building and checking

The charts, the counts and the re-run.

Largest

Planning and judgement

Settling definitions and writing the answer.

Doesn't all that cost more?

Not for this one. As a rough estimate from assumed step counts, it comes to about $1.00 orchestrated, against about $2.20 in one chat on the largest model. It also finishes sooner, because the two builders run together. That's an estimate, not a measurement.

  • Shorter chats get re-read less: about 1.2M tokens in total instead of 3.2M. A token is roughly a word.
  • The building is done on a model that costs half as much.
  • The first look at the data is done on one that costs a fortieth as much.
Show the math
Dollars per million tokens. First-party list prices as of November 2026; your organisation's rates may differ.
ModelRead, newWrittenRe-read
Largest (Opus 5.5)$4$20$0.20
Mid-sized (Sonnet 5.5)$2$10$0.10
Small (Haiku 5.5)$0.10$0.50not used

We assume text read for the first time is stored so it can be re-read cheaply, at 1.25 times the read price. That makes new material $5.00 per million on the largest model and $2.50 on the mid-sized one.

One chat

Largest model only

About 40 steps. The chat grows from about 15,000 to about 150,000 tokens, so each step re-reads about 80,000 on average.

  • Re-reading: 40 × 80,000 = 3.2M tokens × $0.20 = $0.64
  • New material read (data peeks, results, errors): 135,000 × $5.00 = $0.68
  • Written (code, reasoning, the report): 45,000 × $20 = $0.90
  • Total: about $2.20

Orchestrated

Largest plans, smaller build

  • Planner, largest model, about 12 steps at about 25,000 tokens: re-reading 0.3M × $0.20 = $0.06; new 20,000 × $5.00 = $0.10; written 8,000 × $20 = $0.16. About $0.32
  • Reader, small model: 60,000 read, 3,000 written. About $0.01
  • Builder A, mid-sized, about 15 steps at about 30,000: re-reading 0.45M × $0.10 = $0.05; new 40,000 × $2.50 = $0.10; written 15,000 × $10 = $0.15. About $0.30
  • Builder B, mid-sized: the same. About $0.30
  • Checker, mid-sized: about $0.10
  • Total: about $1.00

The honest part

It doesn't remove work, it moves it to shorter chats and cheaper models. For a question one chart can answer, one chat is cheaper. And the planner settles what "high-cost" means before anyone builds, because a small model shouldn't be the one deciding that.

What keeps it from going off the rails?

You stay in charge. The work also happens on a branch, a separate copy of the project's history, until you accept it. And none of this depends on one vendor's assistant.

  • Nothing gets built until you say yes to a short plan.
  • Each helper is told which files it may touch.
  • Automatic fix rounds have a fixed limit, so it can't loop.
